---
title: "Conditional means"
---

The earlier discussion of [conditional expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd) defined an expected value within a specified condition. Regression uses that same object while allowing the conditioning value to vary.

Suppose a self-paced reading study records reading time at each word. Let

$$
Y_i=\text{log reading time for word }i
$$

and let

$$
X_i=\text{surprisal of word }i\text{ in bits}.
$$

Surprisal measures how unexpected the word was under a specified language model. A processing account may predict that more surprising words take longer to read.

## Beginning with one predictor value

Consider words with surprisal 4 bits. Their reading times vary, so the model should not assign one inevitable response to every such word.

Instead, we can ask for the expected response among observations with that predictor value:

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=4].
$$

This is a [**conditional mean**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html). It is the center of the response distribution restricted to words with surprisal 4.

Now consider 5 bits:

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=5].
$$

If the second quantity is larger, expected log reading time increases with surprisal.

## Treating the conditional mean as a function

Let the predictor value vary:

$$
m(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x].
$$

The function $m$ maps every predictor value $x$ to the expected response at that value.

A [**regression model**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-reg.html) specifies a form for this conditional distribution. Its central location may change with $x$, and in richer models its scale or shape may change as well.

## Comparing conditional and marginal means

The marginal mean

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]
$$

averages over words with every surprisal value. It does not describe how reading time changes across surprisal.

The conditional mean preserves that distinction. It lets us compare the response distribution at 4 bits with the distribution at 5 bits.

## Stating the regression question precisely

For this study, the question is

> How does expected log reading time at a word change as that word's surprisal changes?

Surprisal is treated as a supplied predictor. Estimating the language model that produced it is a separate inferential task.

The conditional association also need not be causal. Frequency, word length, contextual constraint, and other properties may vary with surprisal. A causal interpretation requires design and identification assumptions beyond the regression equation.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the target"}
Why does $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=4]=6$ not imply that every word with surprisal 4 has log reading time 6?
:::

The [next page](simple-linear-regression.qmd) makes one first assumption about $m(x)$: it is a straight line.
